title: 28. Development of a pipeline to enhance the competitiveness of underrepresented scholars for entry into agriculture, scientific and professional careers.
content:
Abstract
The objective of this project was to enhance access to graduate training and increase the competitiveness of Hispanic and other underrepresented students for entry into agricultural, scientific, and professional careers through a structured, inter-institutional pipeline between New Mexico State University (NMSU) and California State University, Chico (Chico). The program targeted third and fourth-year undergraduates and M.S. graduate students in animal science and related disciplines and emphasized experiential learning, faculty and peer mentoring, professional development, and cross-institutional collaboration. Participants were recruited through coursework outreach, application review, and interviews, and were required to maintain a minimum 2.5 grade point average. Students were paired with faculty mentors and integrated into research laboratories, participating in weekly lab meetings and quarterly professional development seminars conducted jointly between institutions. Program evaluation employed a mixed-methods approach including annual recruitment and retention tracking, demographic monitoring, pre- and post-self-assessments of leadership and professional competencies, mentor assessments, focus groups, and follow-up surveys. Pre- and post-surveys utilized a Likert scale (1 = completely uncertain; 6 = completely certain) to evaluate competencies of student experience. Survey responses were summarized using frequency distributions. A total of 24 undergraduate (NMSU = 10, Chico = 14) and six graduate (NMSU = 5, Chico = 1) students have participated in the program from 2022 to 2026. End-of-year three evaluation data demonstrated measurable gains in student confidence across multiple agricultural competencies: specifically, technical skillset necessary for the agriculture field, their ability to work effectively with professionals from different disciplines, increased confidence in applying course content to real-world, applications, and teamwork. Additionally, this program supported 11 research project presentations at professional or industry conferences and one scientific journal publication. Five participants have been employed by industry and six of the undergraduates are enrolled in an M.S. program at either NMSU or another institution. Qualitative feedback indicated that research engagement, graduate school exposure, cross-campus networking, and one-on-one mentorship were the most impactful program components. Results of this program indicate that a structured, cohort-based, experiential pipeline model significantly strengthens technical confidence, interdisciplinary teamwork skills, graduate school preparedness, and leadership development among underrepresented students in Food and Agricultural Sciences. This model demonstrates effectiveness in building a sustainable HSI-to-graduate-school pipeline and has strong potential for replication at peer institutions.
